quizName: DMV Practice Test #11 25 Questions • Passing Score 20

questions.question: Motorcycles are hard to see at night. What should a motorcycle rider do?

options.text: Sound the horn repeatedly at night.
Stay directly in front of another vehicle to be seen in their headlights.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride slower at night.
questions.explanation: Ride slower at night, increase your distance from other vehicles, use the headlights of cars ahead to see farther, use your high beam (unless meeting another vehicle), and adjust your lane position.

questions.question: In group riding, what does this hand signal mean?
questions.correctAnswerText: Stop.
questions.explanation: Hand signals help riders communicate in groups. When the lead rider extends their left arm down with their palm facing back, all riders should stop.

questions.question: If another driver is following you too closely, what should you do?

options.text: Change lanes and let them pass.

questions.correctAnswerText: Change lanes and let them pass.
questions.explanation: The best solution is to let them pass. Change lanes safely and let the tailgating driver go ahead. Speeding up may cause them to tailgate you at an even higher speed.

questions.question: Where is the engine cut-off switch on a motorcycle?
questions.correctAnswerText: Near the right handgrip
questions.explanation: The engine cut-off switch is usually next to the right handgrip. Know where all your motorcycle's controls are before you ride.

questions.question: How do you get the shortest stopping distance in a straight line?

options.text: Use both brakes without locking either wheel.
Use both brakes and lock the rear wheel.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use both brakes without locking either wheel.
questions.explanation: Use both brakes to stop in the shortest distance on a straight road. Avoid locking either brake.

questions.question: When should you adjust your rearview mirrors?
questions.correctAnswerText: Before starting the motorcycle
questions.explanation: Clean and adjust both mirrors before you start your motorcycle. Adjust them so you can see the lane behind you and as much of the next lane as possible.

questions.question: What is true about more than half of all motorcycle crashes?

options.text: The rider had less than six months of experience on that motorcycle.
They are caused by faulty ignition systems.
They happen because of distractions from passengers.

questions.correctAnswerText: The rider had less than six months of experience on that motorcycle.
questions.explanation: Be very careful when riding a motorcycle that is new to you. Most motorcycle crashes happen with riders who have less than six months of experience on that bike.

questions.question: When should you increase your following distance?

options.text: When you can see through the vehicle in front of you.

questions.correctAnswerText: When the road is wet.
questions.explanation: Increase your distance from the vehicle ahead when your motorcycle needs more space to stop. Also increase your distance in heavy traffic or when you can't see through the vehicle in front of you.

questions.question: Where is the throttle on a motorcycle?
questions.correctAnswerText: On the right handgrip
questions.explanation: The throttle is on the right handgrip. Know where all your motorcycle's controls are before you ride.

questions.question: What is true about the front brake?

options.text: It provides less than half of the motorcycle's braking power.
It provides about 70 percent of the motorcycle's braking power.
Use it only when the road is wet.
It should be the only brake you use.

questions.correctAnswerText: It provides about 70 percent of the motorcycle's braking power.
questions.explanation: The front brake is much more powerful than the rear brake. It provides at least 70 percent of your motorcycle's total stopping power. Use both brakes every time you slow down or stop.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a hazard when another vehicle passes you?
questions.correctAnswerText: Headlights.
questions.explanation: When being passed, watch out for the passing vehicle's mirrors, wind gusts, and objects thrown by passengers. These are real hazards. Headlights are not a hazard when another vehicle passes you.

questions.question: What should you do to reduce your risk of crashing?

options.text: Use your turn signals when changing lanes.
Look only 15 feet ahead of your motorcycle.
Don't use your headlight during the day.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use your turn signals when changing lanes.
questions.explanation: To reduce crash risk, use your turn signals to show other drivers your plans. Also stay visible, keep safe distance, look ahead at least 12 seconds, spot hazards, and be ready to react.

questions.question: Why is riding directly beside another vehicle dangerous?

options.text: You may have trouble reaching a highway exit.
You may be in the other vehicle's blind spot.
You may block the driver's view.
It prevents other drivers from passing both of you.

questions.correctAnswerText: You may be in the other vehicle's blind spot.
questions.explanation: Riding alongside another vehicle is dangerous because you could be in its blind spot. The driver may move into your lane without seeing you. The vehicle also blocks your escape route if danger appears.

questions.question: What is the best way to handle a tailgater?

options.text: Move onto the shoulder to get out of their way.
Speed up to put distance between you and them.
Change lanes and let them pass.

questions.correctAnswerText: Change lanes and let them pass.
questions.explanation: The best way to handle a tailgater is to get them in front of you. If you can do it safely, change lanes and let them pass. Speeding up may make them follow faster and increase danger.

questions.question: When do most crashes happen?
questions.correctAnswerText: On short trips.
questions.explanation: Most crashes happen on trips shorter than five miles, just a few minutes after you start riding.

questions.question: What do goggles protect when riding?

options.text: Your eyes, but not your face.
Your face, but not your eyes.
Your eyes less well than eyeglasses.

questions.correctAnswerText: Your eyes, but not your face.
questions.explanation: Goggles protect your eyes but not your entire face. Only a face shield protects your whole face. Eyeglasses do not work as well as goggles or a face shield.

questions.question: How should you hold the handgrips when riding over rough surfaces?

options.text: Hold them loosely to allow movement.
Hold them firmly to maintain control.
Use lots of throttle to get over the rough surface.
Ride without a helmet so it doesn't cover your face.

questions.correctAnswerText: Hold them firmly to maintain control.
questions.explanation: Hold the handgrips firmly when riding over rough surfaces. This keeps your motorcycle under control.

questions.question: What is true about the front brake?

options.text: Use it only when you need to stop quickly.
Use it only on slippery surfaces.
It is not as effective as the rear brake.
It is safe to use if used properly.

questions.correctAnswerText: It is safe to use if used properly.
questions.explanation: Use both brakes every time you slow down or stop. The front brake is more powerful than the rear brake and is safe to use when used correctly.

questions.question: Before riding, which tire feature should you NOT check?

options.text: The reflective quality of your tires.

questions.correctAnswerText: The reflective quality of your tires.
questions.explanation: Before every ride, check your tires' air pressure, tread wear, and the general condition of the sidewalls and tread.

questions.question: What type of sign is yellow with black lettering or symbols?
questions.correctAnswerText: Warning
questions.explanation: Warning signs are yellow with black lettering or symbols. They alert drivers to upcoming road conditions.

questions.question: A plastic, shatter-resistant face shield:

options.text: Is not necessary if you have a windshield.
Protects your entire face, not just your eyes.
Does not protect your face as well as goggles.

questions.correctAnswerText: Protects your entire face, not just your eyes.
questions.explanation: A face shield protects your whole face, including your eyes. Goggles only protect your eyes. A windshield is not enough protection.

questions.question: When carrying a passenger or cargo:

options.text: Speeding up takes less time, but stopping takes more time.
Speeding up and stopping both take more time.
Speeding up takes more time, but stopping takes less time.
Speeding up and stopping both take less time.

questions.correctAnswerText: Speeding up and stopping both take more time.
questions.explanation: Extra weight from a passenger or cargo makes your motorcycle slower to speed up and slower to stop.

questions.question: When riding with a passenger, you should:
questions.correctAnswerText: Ride slower than usual.
questions.explanation: A passenger adds weight, which lowers your motorcycle and makes it harder to control. Ride slower, especially in curves and corners. The extra weight also means your motorcycle takes longer to speed up or stop, so keep more distance between you and other vehicles.

questions.question: If you find yourself riding directly beside another vehicle, you should:

options.text: Stay alongside until the next exit.
Let the other driver worry about it.

questions.correctAnswerText: Speed up or slow down.
questions.explanation: Riding beside another vehicle is dangerous. You could be in the vehicle's blind spot. If another hazard appears, the vehicle could block your escape route. Either speed up or drop back.

questions.question: An advantage to keeping space between your motorcycle and other vehicles is:

options.text: You can pass danger more quickly.
You will have a narrower view of the road to stay focused.
You will have more time to react to what other drivers do.
You can more easily follow the path of the next vehicle.

questions.correctAnswerText: You will have more time to react to what other drivers do.
questions.explanation: Space between vehicles gives you a clearer view of hazards. You have more time to react and more room to maneuver.
